Saʿīd ibn Jubayr al-Asadī al-Kūfī (45–95 AH). When ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ashʿath rebelled against al-Ḥajjāj in Iraq during the caliphate of the Umayyad ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān, Saʿīd joined the revolt because of his anger at al-Ḥajjāj’s tyranny. After Ibn al-Ashʿath was defeated and killed, Saʿīd went to Mecca. The governor there, Khālid al-Qasrī, arrested him and sent him to al-Ḥajjāj, who had him killed. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said: “al-Ḥajjāj killed Saʿīd when there was no one on the face of the earth who was not in need of his knowledge.” Muḥammad Asʿad Ṭalas, Tārīkh al-Umma al-ʿArabiyya, Beirut, 198, vol. 2, p. 126.↩︎

In Arabic, zahida fī al-shayʾ or zahida ʿanhu means to turn away from something and leave it. Thus zahida fī al-dunyā means to renounce worldly life in order to devote oneself to worship.↩︎

They interpreted the verse, “Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world, but lasting good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope” (Qurʾan 18:46), as proof that worldly life itself was worthless and as a justification for despising and abandoning it in pursuit of “lasting good deeds.”↩︎

The contradiction between asceticism and Qadarism comes from the fact that asceticism depends on trusting in God’s decree and destiny, while the Qadarites rejected the deterministic meaning of that trust. The contradiction between the ascetics and the traditionalists comes from the ascetics allowing themselves to interpret Islamic texts in ways that fit their own way of life. The traditionalists rejected this because they insisted on the plain and direct meanings of the texts.↩︎

The Sufis claim that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was the first Sufi and the pioneer of Sufism. In reality, neither his conduct nor his thought went beyond the asceticism of his own time in either character or content. Indeed, in practice he may be counted among the more moderate ascetics, since he did not go to extremes in seclusion or worship. He is famous for saying: “An atom’s weight of sound piety is better than a thousand weights of fasting and prayer” (al-Risāla al-Qushayriyya, p. 54). Despite the simplicity and conventional Islamic meaning of this statement, later Sufis treated it as evidence that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was one of them, or even their pioneer. Yet ordinary Muslim believers say the same thing, as do the leading scholars of Sunni Islam and the jurists, especially—even when they are hostile to Sufism.↩︎
